reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: The rarest of the eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders in adults, with a bimodal age distribution affecting infants and adults.
The infantile form (allergic proctocolitis) is typically benign, cow's milk protein-related and resolves with dietary change.
The adult form presents with diarrhoea, abdominal pain and sometimes rectal bleeding, and is often idiopathic.
Physiological colonic eosinophil counts vary by site, being higher in the caecum and right colon, so biopsies must be interpreted against regional norms.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out parasites, drugs, inflammatory bowel disease, connective tissue disease, hypereosinophilic syndrome and malignancy.
Peripheral eosinophilia is less consistent than in upper gastrointestinal eosinophilic disorders.
Treatment is dietary elimination in infants and corticosteroids or other agents in persistent adult disease.
Multiple biopsies across colonic segments are required to make the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophilic colitis is an eosinophilic infiltration of the colonic mucosa, and sometimes deeper layers, driven by Th2 allergic mechanisms that are most clearly food-antigen (cow's milk protein) related in infants. Eosinophil recruitment and degranulation cause mucosal inflammation, altered motility and secretory diarrhoea. Because baseline colonic eosinophil density is normally high and regionally variable, distinguishing pathological infiltration from physiological presence is central and challenging.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease)
Cow's milk protein allergy in infants
additionalInvestigations: Ileocolonoscopy with segmental biopsies and eosinophil counts against regional norms
Full blood count with eosinophil count
Stool microscopy and serology for parasites
Allergy assessment where food allergy is suspected
Cross-sectional imaging if wall thickening or a mass is present
Screen for hypereosinophilic syndrome and vasculitis where indicated
redFlags: Weight loss or failure to thrive in infants
Features suggesting inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy or systemic vasculitis
Severe or refractory diarrhoea with dehydration
reference.prognosis: Infantile allergic proctocolitis has an excellent prognosis and usually resolves with dietary modification, whereas adult eosinophilic colitis is more variable and often relapsing but is generally not life-threatening.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosis by ignoring the normal regional variation in colonic eosinophils
Missing an underlying parasitic infection or drug cause
Labelling inflammatory bowel disease-related eosinophilia as primary eosinophilic colitis
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
International consensus nomenclature for eosinophilic gastrointestinal diseases
management: In infantile allergic proctocolitis, eliminate cow's milk protein, using maternal dietary exclusion in breastfed infants or an extensively hydrolysed or amino-acid formula
Empirical dietary elimination with structured reintroduction to identify food triggers in older children and adults
Corticosteroids, including targeted budesonide, for symptomatic adult disease not controlled by diet
Exclude and treat secondary causes such as parasites, drugs and inflammatory bowel disease before settling on the diagnosis
Steroid-sparing immunomodulators or anti-eosinophil biologics for relapsing or steroid-dependent disease
Monitor symptoms, colonic histology and growth in children, with gastroenterology referral
Reassure families about the benign, self-limiting course of the infantile form
